tips.title: One mechanism, both trends
tips.body: Down a group the atom is bigger and more shielded, so attraction is **weaker**. Group 1 **loses** — so easier, **more** reactive. Group 7 **gains** — so harder, **less** reactive. Learn the mechanism and you can never get them the wrong way round.

tips.title: Helium has two, not eight

tips.title: Ionic with metals, covalent with non-metals

tips.title: Predict with the trend, not just the value
tips.body: *Predict properties from given trends* appears in all three group spec points. Give the prediction **and** the trend it rests on — *above −153 °C, because boiling point rises with relative atomic mass down the group*.

steps.title: Group 0: the noble gases
steps.body:
**The elements in Group 0 are called the noble gases.**

**They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules, because their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons.**

That is the explanation, and it is worth being precise about: a noble gas is unreactive **because its outer shell is already full**. Reactions happen when atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach a full outer shell — and a noble gas has nothing to gain by reacting.

**The noble gases have eight electrons in their outer shell, except for helium, which has only two.**

Helium is the exception because the **first shell holds only two electrons**. Helium's shell is full with two — it is just as stable, with a different number. An answer saying *all noble gases have eight outer electrons* is wrong, and the marker is looking for the exception.

**The trend: the boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass**, which means they increase **going down the group**.

**Why.** The atoms get **bigger and heavier** down the group, so the **forces between the atoms** get stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. Note this is about forces **between** atoms, not about bonding **within** anything — noble gases exist as **single atoms**, which is itself a consequence of being unreactive.

**Predicting from the trend** is something the spec asks for directly. If argon boils at −186 °C and krypton at −153 °C, then xenon, being further down, must boil **above −153 °C**.

steps.title: Group 1: the alkali metals
steps.body:
**The elements in Group 1 are known as the alkali metals, and have characteristic properties because of the single electron in their outer shell.**

One outer electron, easily lost, forming a **1+ ion**. Everything about Group 1 follows from that.

**You should be able to describe the reactions of the first three alkali metals — lithium, sodium and potassium — with oxygen, chlorine and water.**

**With oxygen**, they tarnish quickly and burn to form an **oxide**:

$$\mathrm{4Li + O_2 \rightarrow 2Li_2O}$$

**With chlorine**, they burn to form a **chloride**, a white ionic solid:

$$\mathrm{2Na + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2NaCl}$$

**With water**, they react to give a **hydroxide** and **hydrogen**:

$$\mathrm{2Na + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_2}$$

The solution formed is **alkaline** — which is where the name *alkali metals* comes from.

**What you see, going down the group:**

- **Lithium** fizzes steadily on the surface of water.
- **Sodium** melts into a ball from the heat released, and moves rapidly about.
- **Potassium** reacts violently, and the hydrogen produced **ignites** with a lilac flame.

**In Group 1, the reactivity of the elements increases going down the group.** The observations above are that trend, seen directly.

steps.title: Group 7: the halogens
steps.body:
**The elements in Group 7 are known as the halogens, and have similar reactions because they all have seven electrons in their outer shell.**

**The halogens are non-metals and consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms** — they are **diatomic**: $\mathrm{F_2}$, $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, $\mathrm{Br_2}$, $\mathrm{I_2}$. Writing chlorine as *Cl* in an equation is a common and costly slip.

**The compounds they form** depend on what they react with, and the spec asks for both:

- **With metals**, they form **ionic** compounds. The halogen **gains one electron** to become a **halide ion** with a **1− charge**: sodium chloride, magnesium bromide.
- **With non-metals**, they form **covalent, molecular** compounds, in which electrons are **shared**: hydrogen chloride, carbon tetrachloride.

**The trends down Group 7:**

- **The further down the group, the higher the relative molecular mass, melting point and boiling point.** So at room temperature chlorine is a **gas**, bromine a **liquid** and iodine a **solid**.
- **The reactivity of the elements decreases going down the group** — the **opposite** of Group 1.

**Displacement.** **A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt.** So chlorine displaces bromine and iodine; bromine displaces iodine; and iodine displaces **neither**.

$$\mathrm{Cl_2 + 2KBr \rightarrow 2KCl + Br_2}$$

This is a useful test of the reactivity order, because you can **see** it: the colourless solution turns orange as bromine is released.

steps.title: Why the trends run in opposite directions
steps.body:
Group 1 gets **more** reactive going down; Group 7 gets **less**. That looks like two facts to learn. It is **one** explanation, applied twice.

**What changes going down any group:**

1. There are **more shells**, so the atom is **bigger**.
2. The **outer electrons are further from the nucleus**.
3. There is more **shielding** by the inner shells of electrons.
4. So the **attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons is weaker**.

**Now apply that to each group:**

**Group 1 loses an electron.** Weaker attraction means the outer electron is **held less tightly**, so it is **easier to lose**. Easier to lose means **more reactive**. So reactivity **increases** down Group 1.

**Group 7 gains an electron.** Weaker attraction means an incoming electron is **attracted less strongly**, so it is **harder to gain**. Harder to gain means **less reactive**. So reactivity **decreases** down Group 7.

$$\textbf{same cause} \rightarrow \textbf{opposite effect, because one loses and the other gains}$$

**That is the highest-value idea in the topic.** A student who has memorised two trends can state them; a student who has this can **derive** them, and can apply the same reasoning to any group they meet.

**In an answer, give the chain.** *Going down the group the atoms are bigger, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so the attraction is weaker, so it is more easily lost, so the element is more reactive.* Each link is a mark.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**One mechanism, two trends.** Going down a group the atom is **bigger**, the outer shell is **further from the nucleus** and **more shielded**, so the attraction is **weaker**. Group 1 **loses**, so weaker attraction makes it **easier** — more reactive. Group 7 **gains**, so weaker attraction makes it **harder** — less reactive. Learn the mechanism and both trends come out; learn the trends and you have nothing to fall back on when you forget which way round they go.

**Helium has two outer electrons, not eight.** The **first shell holds only two**, so helium's shell is full with two. Writing *all noble gases have eight* is a standard lost mark, and it is the exception that questions are built around.

**Halogens are diatomic.** $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, not $\mathrm{Cl}$. Writing the wrong one unbalances every equation it appears in, and the error propagates through the rest of the answer.

**Ionic with metals, covalent with non-metals.** The halogen **gains** an electron from a metal — giving a **1− halide ion** — and **shares** with a non-metal. A question asking about *the nature of the compounds formed* is asking for exactly this distinction, and it wants both halves.

**Displacement is a visible test of the order.** Chlorine added to potassium bromide solution turns it orange as bromine is released. So the reactivity series is not asserted — it is **demonstrated**, and each displacement that happens, and each that does not, is evidence.

**Noble gases exist as single atoms**, and that is a consequence rather than a separate fact: they do not easily form molecules because their electron arrangements are already stable. So when explaining their boiling points, the forces involved are **between atoms**, not within molecules.

**Predicting is a marked skill in its own right.** *Predict properties from given trends down the group* appears in all three group spec points. If argon boils at −186 °C and krypton at −153 °C, then xenon boils **above −153 °C** — and the reason to give is that boiling point **increases with relative atomic mass down the group**. Give the prediction **and** the trend it rests on.

**The name is a clue.** *Alkali* metals produce **alkaline** hydroxide solutions with water. **Halogen** comes from *salt-former* — they form salts with metals. Names in chemistry usually record a property, and noticing that makes them easier to keep straight.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Group 0: the noble gases.** Unreactive, and they **do not easily form molecules**, because their atoms have **stable arrangements of electrons**.
- Noble gases have **eight** outer electrons — **except helium, which has two**, because the first shell holds only two.
- **Boiling points increase** with increasing relative atomic mass, that is **down the group**.
- **Group 1: the alkali metals.** Their properties come from the **single outer electron**, lost to form a **1+ ion**.
- With **oxygen** → a **metal oxide**. With **chlorine** → a **metal chloride**. With **water** → a **metal hydroxide and hydrogen**.
- $\mathrm{2Na + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_2}$ — the solution is **alkaline**.
- Lithium **fizzes**, sodium **melts into a ball**, potassium **ignites** with a lilac flame.
- **Group 1 reactivity increases going down.**
- **Group 7: the halogens.** Seven outer electrons, so similar reactions. **Non-metals**, existing as **diatomic molecules**: $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, not $\mathrm{Cl}$.
- With **metals** → **ionic** compounds, the halogen gaining one electron to form a **1− halide ion**.
- With **non-metals** → **covalent, molecular** compounds.
- Down Group 7, **relative molecular mass, melting point and boiling point all increase**: chlorine gas, bromine liquid, iodine solid.
- **Group 7 reactivity decreases going down.**
- **A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one** from a solution of its salt.
- **One mechanism explains both trends**: down a group the atom is bigger, the outer shell further out and more shielded, so attraction is **weaker** — making **losing easier** and **gaining harder**.

questions.prompt: Explain why reactivity increases down Group 1 but decreases down Group 7, using the same reasoning for both.
questions.solution: Both trends follow from a single change that happens going down any group. As you move down a group each successive element has one more occupied electron shell, so the atoms become larger and the outer electrons are further from the nucleus. There are also more inner shells of electrons between the nucleus and the outer shell, which shield the outer electrons from the positive charge of the nucleus. The combined effect is that the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons becomes weaker further down the group. The consequence of this weaker attraction depends entirely on what the group needs to do in order to react. Group 1 elements have a single electron in their outer shell and react by losing it to form a one plus ion. Because the attraction on that outer electron is weaker further down the group, the electron is held less tightly and is therefore easier to lose, so the element reacts more readily and the reactivity increases going down Group 1. Group 7 elements have seven outer electrons and react by gaining one to form a one minus halide ion. Because the attraction from the nucleus is weaker further down the group, an incoming electron is attracted less strongly, so it is harder for the atom to gain one, and the reactivity therefore decreases going down Group 7. The same cause produces opposite effects because one group loses an electron and the other gains one, and this is why it is better to learn the mechanism than to memorise the two trends separately.

questions.modelAnswer:
**One cause, applied twice.**

**Going down any group:**

1. One more **occupied shell**, so the atom is **bigger**.
2. The outer electrons are **further from the nucleus**.
3. More inner shells **shield** them from the nuclear charge.
4. So the **attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons is weaker**.

**Group 1 loses an electron** (one outer electron → 1+ ion). Weaker attraction means it is **held less tightly**, so **easier to lose** → **reactivity increases** down the group.

**Group 7 gains an electron** (seven outer electrons → 1− halide ion). Weaker attraction means an incoming electron is **attracted less strongly**, so it is **harder to gain** → **reactivity decreases** down the group.

**Why the trends oppose.** The **same cause** produces **opposite effects** because **one group loses and the other gains**.

**Each link in that chain is a mark**, so write the chain out rather than jumping to the conclusion — and learning the mechanism means you can never get the two trends the wrong way round.

questions.prompt: Describe the reactions of lithium, sodium and potassium with water, and explain what the observations show.
questions.solution: All three alkali metals react with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. For sodium the equation is two sodium plus two water gives two sodium hydroxide plus hydrogen. The hydroxide dissolves to give an alkaline solution, which is why these elements are called the alkali metals and why the resulting solution turns universal indicator purple. The observations differ markedly between the three. Lithium floats and fizzes steadily on the surface of the water as hydrogen is released, and the reaction is brisk but controlled. Sodium reacts more vigorously, and enough heat is released for the sodium to melt into a ball which moves rapidly about the surface as the escaping hydrogen propels it. Potassium reacts violently, and so much heat is released that the hydrogen produced ignites, burning with a lilac flame characteristic of potassium. These observations show that the reactivity of the elements increases going down Group 1. The explanation is that each element further down the group has one more occupied electron shell, so its outer electron is further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner shells. The attraction between the nucleus and that outer electron is therefore weaker, and since the reaction requires the atom to lose that electron, losing it becomes easier further down the group and the element reacts more readily.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The general reaction:** metal + water → **metal hydroxide + hydrogen**.

$$\mathrm{2Na + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_2}$$

The hydroxide gives an **alkaline** solution — which is where *alkali metals* comes from.

**The observations:**

- **Lithium** — floats and **fizzes steadily** on the surface; brisk but controlled.
- **Sodium** — more vigorous; enough heat is released that it **melts into a ball**, moving rapidly as escaping hydrogen propels it.
- **Potassium** — **violent**; so much heat that the hydrogen **ignites**, burning with a **lilac** flame.

**What they show.** Reactivity **increases going down Group 1**.

**Why.** Each element further down has **one more shell**, so its outer electron is **further from the nucleus** and **more shielded**. The attraction is **weaker**, and since reacting requires **losing** that electron, it becomes **easier** — so the element reacts more readily.

examTechnique.body:
Explain both reactivity trends from the same mechanism: bigger atom, more shielding, weaker attraction.

Say whether the group loses or gains an electron before saying whether reactivity rises or falls.

Give the full chain of reasoning, since each link earns a mark.

Remember that helium has two outer electrons, not eight.

Write halogens as diatomic molecules in every equation.

Distinguish the ionic compounds formed with metals from the covalent ones formed with non-metals.

When predicting a property, state the trend it is based on as well as the value.

Use displacement results as evidence for the reactivity order.
examinerErrors: Saying all noble gases have eight outer electrons.
Writing Cl instead of Cl2 in an equation.
Stating the reactivity trends without explaining them.
Claiming a less reactive halogen displaces a more reactive one.
Saying halogens always form ionic compounds.
Predicting a value without giving the trend it rests on.
Describing the forces between noble gas atoms as covalent bonds.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer derives the two reactivity trends rather than recalling them, from a single chain: bigger atom, outer electrons further out and more shielded, weaker attraction, and then the opposite consequences of losing against gaining. It knows helium is the exception and why, writes halogens as diatomic molecules without prompting, and distinguishes the ionic compounds formed with metals from the covalent ones formed with non-metals. It treats displacement as evidence for the order rather than as a separate fact, and when asked to predict it gives the trend as well as the number.
